Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 1:

(p-1) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat Fatir, also called Surat al-Mala'ika (the Surah of the Angels).

It is the conclusion of the surahs that open with "al-Hamd" (All praise is due to Allah). It has been mentioned from Shaykh Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani that in it the four blessings are detailed, which are the mothers of the blessings gathered in al-Fatiha (the Opening): the first origination (*al-ijad al-awwal*); then the first sustaining (*al-ibqa' al-awwal*); then the second origination, alluded to in Surat Saba'; then the second sustaining, which is the final and most perfect of them, and its matter is detailed in it, concerning the two groups of happiness and wretchedness, in a thorough explanation. This is in addition to its having completed the four blessings in this surah, as will be explained in its places. Its purpose is therefore the establishment of Allah's complete power (exalted is He), from which necessarily follows the complete power over resurrection, by which the more perfect of the two sustainings comes about: the sustaining in actuality, forever and ever, without cessation, without ending, and without interruption, in the abode of permanence, from which grief, fatigue and weariness have been removed, and the abode of wretchedness, which gathers all distresses and anxieties.

(p-2) The name of the surah has the most complete suitability to its purpose, because nothing equals what is in Paradise of the renewal of creation: nothing of its food is eaten but it returns as it was in the moment, and nothing is willed but it comes into being in the swiftest time. Thus it is truly the abode of innovation and invention. Likewise the Fire: "Whenever their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins" (Q. 4:56). Likewise its naming of the angels as "al-Mala'ika": they are originated anew, each one in the form which Allah willed for him to be, neither increased in it nor decreased, whenever Allah wills that, without any cause at all, apart from His will which accords with His power, glory be to Him and exalted is His majesty. They are among the unbelievers, in a manner that cannot be encompassed: "None knows the hosts of your Lord except Him" (Q. 74:31).

"In the name of Allah" (Allah, the One whose power encircles all possibilities). "The Most Gracious" (the One who by resurrection completed the generality of mercy). "The Most Merciful" (the One who honoured the people of dignity with the permanence of their dwelling in the abode of permanence).

Since, in the surah before it, He (glory be to Him) established the gathering (*al-hashr*), which is the second origination, and indicated it through particular instances of power over things in the cosmos, until He concluded with the seizing of the unbelievers, a seizing that compelled them to faith by making praise manifest to them in the fullest manifestation, and by barring them from everything they desired, just as they had been given enjoyment in this world of most of what they desired, such as abundance of wealth and children, together with the ease that accompanies them, which is among the greatest of distresses; and since praise can come by withholding and destruction as it comes by giving and bestowal, He (exalted is He) said, as the result of that: "Praise" (i.e., the encompassing of the attributes of perfection, in destruction and in origination) "is for Allah" (i.e., Him alone).

(p-3) And since origination from nothingness is more indicative of this, He said, showing that He deserves praises: "Originator (*fatir*) of the heavens and the earth" (i.e., the initiator and innovator of them), meaning the One who was previously established to have all that is in them; by splitting nothingness and bringing them forth from it at the beginning, without any preceding model, as you witness. And since the angels, singular and plural, are like the two horizons (*al-khafiqayn*) in that each of them is originated from nothingness, without any preceding model, without material, and since it had been stated before that they will disown the worship of the unbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, and since there is no path for the common people to knowing them except through report, He informed about them after informing about what is known by observation, with the truth of their condition. So He said, explaining through their variation in forms the completeness of His power and that it is by choice: "Who made the angels messengers" (i.e., as He willed of His purpose, and to whatever of His servants He willed, visible to the prophets among them and to whoever attached himself to them, and not visible), "possessing wings" (i.e., they are equipped for what is required of them). Then He described the wings, saying: "two, two" (i.e., two wings each, for whoever does not need more than that in what he is employed in). Perhaps its mention is to alert to the fact that this is the least that can be, like the two hands. And since that was a pair, He drew attention to the fact that it is not restricted to a pair, so He said: "and three" (i.e., three each, for others among them). And since, had He restricted Himself to that, it would have been thought that the limit lies there, He drew attention (p-4) by mentioning the pair of the pair, to the fact that the increase is not confined, so He said: "and four" (i.e., four each, for each one of another kind among them).

And since it was established by this that He acts by choice, not by nature or anything else, for otherwise things would have to be undifferentiated while their relation to the agent is uniform, the result of that was: "He adds to creation" (i.e., created things), from distinct things, and from the states of the angels; and lightness of spirit, subtlety, heaviness, density; beauty of voice and renown; eloquence and simplicity; cunning and generosity; miserliness; elevation of aspiration and its lowness; and other things that return to quantity and quality, which none other than Him, glory be to Him, can encompass. Thus the claim of whoever said that He finished creation on the seventh day, when He completed the creation of Adam, so that no increase remains, is refuted, as the Jews and others said. Moreover, this doctrine is weak and feeble to an extent that is not hidden. Yet He (glory be to Him) made all the ways clear and left no ambiguity in any of them: "He creates whatever He wills" (so it is no novelty that He should bring into being another abode, which will be for the requital of the servants). Then He explained all of that by His saying, emphasizing it because of their denial of resurrection: "Indeed Allah" (i.e., the One who gathers all the attributes of perfection) "is over all things Competent" (so He is capable of resurrection, and will surely do it).

(p-5) Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When Surat Saba' made clear that He (glory be to Him) is the Owner of the heavens and the earth, and deserves praise in this world and the Hereafter, this surah made clear that this is His creation just as it is His dominion, and that He is the one worthy of praise and deserving of it, since everything is His creation and His dominion. And because the first surah was devoted to making the servants know that all belongs to Him, both creation and dominion, its verses revolve around making known the immensity of His dominion. He gave David and Solomon (peace be upon them both) what is like a drop in the surging seas: iron was made soft for them, and the winds, beasts, birds, jinn and humans were subjugated and submissive: "Say: Call upon those you claim besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have any share in them, nor is any of them a helper to Him" (Q. 34:22). Exalted is our Lord above any helper, partner or equal, and holy is His dominion, beyond what minds can confine or understandings encompass. So Surat Saba' was devoted to making the servants know His immense dominion, glory be to Him, and this other surah was devoted to making known invention and creation. What confirms this is the continuation of the verses of Surat Fatir upon this purpose of making known, and its alerting to beginnings, such as His saying: "Who made the angels messengers, possessing wings, two, three and four" (the verse, etc.), and His saying: "Whatever mercy Allah opens for the people, none can withhold it" (Q. 35:2), "Is there any creator other than Allah who provides for you?" (Q. 35:3), and His saying: "Is one whose evil deed is made attractive to him so that he sees it as good...?" (Q. 35:8, etc.), and His saying: "It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds" (Q. 35:9, etc.), "Allah created you from dust" (Q. 35:11), "He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night" (Q. 35:13), "Do you not see that Allah sends down water from the sky, and We produce with it fruits of varying colours?" (Q. 35:27), "It is He who made you successors upon the earth" (Q. 35:39), "Indeed Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease; and if they should cease, none could hold them after Him" (Q. 35:41). These are a number of verses that make known the beginning of creation and invention, or allude to it, whereas in Surat Saba' there is not a single verse of this kind. Furthermore, the verses of Surat Saba' proceed along the method of making known dominion, its disposal, exclusive control of it, and its unrestricted authority. Consider its opening, the story of David and Solomon (peace be upon them both), and His saying (glory be to Him): "Say: Call upon those you claim besides Allah; they do not possess an atom's weight" (Q. 34:22), and the verses that follow; the matter will become clear to you, as we have mentioned, and whatever seemed to depart from these two aims in the two surahs is connected and called for by the logic of the flow, according to what the purposes of the verses require. May Allah grant us understanding of it, by His bounty and generosity. Ended.

When He, glorified is He, described His sacred Self as possessing complete power, He demonstrated this through what everyone observes within themselves of expansion and constriction, together with their inability to repel any of that or to seize it. So He said, beginning a new statement or giving a causal explanation with a conclusion: ﴿Whatever﴾, that is, whatever it may be, ﴿Allah opens﴾, that is, He who has no equal. Since everything in existence exists for the sake of people, He said: ﴿to the people﴾. And since bestowal is intended for its own sake and is loved, and since His mercy, glorified is He, has overcome His wrath, He stated this explicitly. He said, making the condition explicit in the position of a circumstance relating to the pronoun in it, meaning "He opens it as something existing": ﴿of mercy﴾, that is, of sustenance, both sensory and immaterial, of subtleties and knowledge, which cannot be counted, whether fine or great, so He sends it. ﴿None can withhold it﴾, that is, the mercy, after He has opened it, as everyone knows within themselves: that if some good comes to them, there is never a lack of someone who wishes it had not come, and even if he were able to remove it, he would remove it, yet he has no power to affect what is in it.

Since withholding a blessing is disliked, He did not state it explicitly, and He left the condition in its generality after having explained the first condition as mercy, indicating greater concern for it and signaling that His mercy precedes His wrath. So He said: ﴿And whatever He withholds﴾, that is, of mercy or blessing, by closing the door of creation to it, ﴿none can release it﴾, that is, the one who withheld it, by a proof like the one that preceded regarding mercy.

Since someone might perhaps claim, out of wickedness, during a time when mercy or retribution is withheld, that he himself is the one withholding, He said: ﴿after Him﴾, that is, after His withholding. Thus whoever has something in his hand, let him withhold what Allah has brought into being at the time of its origination, by annihilating it. And since this is evident in the might that governs human affairs and the wisdom in their management, He generalized, saying: ﴿And He is﴾, that is, He is the doer of that, and the state is that He alone is ﴿the Mighty﴾, that is, the one able to withhold and to release, the one who prevails over everything, and none prevails over Him; ﴿the Wise﴾, who does, in each of withholding, releasing and other things, what His knowledge of it requires, and perfects what He wills according to the laws of wisdom, so that none of it can be undone.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 3:

When he had shown, by what everyone observes within himself, that He alone is the Bestower of favour, He commanded the remembrance of His favour, by acknowledging that it comes from Him; for remembrance leads to gratitude, and it is the tether of what exists and the snare of what is absent and lost. So He said: ﴿O mankind﴾; that is, those who possess the capacity for agitation in general; ﴿remember﴾ with the heart and the tongue; ﴿the favour of Allah﴾; that is, the One who, in reality, has no bestower of favour other than Him. And since His favours are general, overflowing from every direction, He said: ﴿upon you﴾; that is, in repelling what He has repelled of trials and in bestowing what He has bestowed of graces, as has preceded in (the discussion of) al-Fath, and in (His) withholding, ﴿that you may be grateful to Him and not be ungrateful﴾. As for what is specific to the people of Makkah, after they had shared it with the people: their settlement in the Haram, their protection from all nations, and their honouring with the House; and this necessitates that they be the most grateful of people.

When He commanded the remembrance of His favour, He reinforced the acquaintance (with it) by stating that it comes from Him alone, in a manner that showed His might and wisdom. So He said, admonishing the heedless, rebuking the one who denies, and refuting the people of qadar who claimed that they create their own actions, and drawing attention to the favour of the first origination: ﴿Is there any creator﴾ (هَلْ); and since the interrogation carries the meaning of negation, He reinforced it with ﴿min﴾ (مِن), saying: ﴿other than Allah﴾ (مِن خالِقٍ); that is, of the favours and other than them. And since ﴿min﴾ (مِن) is for emphasis, and so ﴿khāliq﴾ (خالِقٍ) is in the position of the nominative, the majority read His saying ﴿ghayru Allāh﴾ (غَيْرُ اللَّهِ) with the nominative; while Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive, following the wording. He expressed it with the Divine Name (Allah) to indicate that He is the one specified with the attributes of perfection.

And since the answer is definitively "No", but rather He alone is the Creator, He said, drawing attention to the favour of the first sustenance: ﴿Who provides for you﴾; that is, He alone. And since the abundance of provision, as is observed, is along with the unity of the source, it indicates greater majesty; He said: ﴿from the heaven and the earth﴾; by rain, plants, and other things. And when He had made clear that He alone is the Provider, the hope of everyone from other than Him was cut off, even from himself; thus sincerity was achieved, and it became settled that He, glorified is He, is the God, alone. So He said: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. Thereby the denunciation applies to the one who worships other than Him, outwardly or inwardly. So He said: ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾; that is, from what direction and how are you turned away and turned about from the path of rectitude in monotheism, by these manifest proofs, to polytheism, which has no justification.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 4:

When He had established them upon what preceded, and concluded with monotheism (*tawhid*, the affirmation of God's oneness), which is the first foundational principle of the religion, He drew attention to the fact that the principle intended in itself is the second foundational principle that follows it, namely the messengership (*risala*, the mission of the prophets), with its affirmation and denial. He said, deploring the bad reception that the Quraysh gave to His signs and their slander against His clear proofs, consoling him (ﷺ), (p-10) and linking it to what its implied sense is: "If they affirm you, they are worthy of affirmation, because of the proofs that stand upon that and the aims and means that bear witness to it": ﴿And if they deny you﴾; that is, out of obstinacy and little concern for the consequences, so be patient, following the example of your brothers; ﴿then indeed﴾; that is, because ﴿messengers were denied﴾ before you; that is, how excellent were those messengers! He put the verb in the passive form because the object of consolation is the occurrence of denial, not the identity of the denier. And He negated that He would send anyone else after His existence (of the Prophet) with His words ﴿before you﴾. He mentioned the denial alone, giving attention to the consolation, as a reminder that most people are denied. Al-Qushayri said: In this there is an indication that the wise and the people of the hearts, together with the common folk and the outsiders, from this path, are such that they accept from them only a few; and the people of realities are always, from them, in enduring harm; and the common folk are closer to this path than the ascetic reciters.

Since the implied sense was a negation of wonder at denial that occurs without sound reasoning: "Then from God, with whom no command belongs to anyone, do affairs proceed," He followed it with His words, threatening those who oppose His command: ﴿And to God﴾; that is, alone, because to Him belong all affairs; ﴿all affairs are returned﴾; that is, in both the tangible and the meaningful sense. So be patient, and refer the matter to Us, by abandoning means except what We command you, as your brothers among the messengers did.

When the closing of the previous verses had signalled the promised Day, which is the firmly established foundation, He said, threatening with it and warning against it: ﴿O mankind﴾; that is, those who have the capacity to be moved toward reflection. Since they were denying the resurrection, He emphasised His statement: ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah﴾; that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, and who is exempt from every trace of deficiency, so that it is not possible for Him, according to the course of customary practice, to break the appointment, because of His absolute self-sufficiency; ﴿is true﴾; that is, in everything He has promised, including the resurrection and other things. He has promised that He will bring you back to Him on a Day when means are cut off, lineage and noble descent are disregarded, and He will judge between you with justice. Then, on the basis of its being true, He made the following statement a consequence, in a manner of emphasis, also for the sake of rejecting denial: ﴿So let not the life of this world deceive you﴾; that is, with the various kinds of deceptions, from amusement and adornment, a deception that is continually renewed. For it does not befit one of lofty aspiration to follow the base and to be content with the lowly, perishable thing instead of the exalted, enduring one. ﴿And let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾; that is, the One who does not break His appointment and who is the Great, the Exalted; ﴿the Deceiver﴾; that is, the one who is not to be believed in anything, and he is the enemy Satan. For this reason He resumed His statement, using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, to create aversion through the meaning of the description, before reminding them of the enmity and the grave outcome of what he calls to, emphasising that the deeds of those who follow him, through what he holds out to them, such as: "Indeed your Lord is Forbearing, no sin is great to Him, despite persistence in disobedience," are the deeds of those who are deluded into befriending him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, Satan﴾; that is, the one burning with anger, far from good; ﴿is an enemy to you﴾; that is, specifically to you. He is entirely free to harm you, so strive to flee from him. ﴿an enemy﴾; by directing all his schemes at you, and by what has already passed between him and your father Adam, peace be upon him, by how his harm has reached you. Also: "Whoever shows enmity to your father, has shown enmity to you." (p. 12) Since his enmity requires striving against him, because he comes to a person through the desires, He expressed it in the form of ifti'al (reflexive form) and said: ﴿So take him﴾; that is, with the utmost of your effort; ﴿as an enemy﴾. Allah is your Protector, so take Him as your Protector: by seeking out what angers Satan, by opposing him in everything he wants and commands, and by deliberately doing what the Most Merciful is pleased with, and what He has laid down for you and commanded you, so that you adhere to it. Al-Qushayri said: "One cannot prevail over his enmity except by constantly seeking help from the Lord, for He does not neglect your enmity, so do not you neglect your Master even for a moment." Then he gave the reason for this in His saying: ﴿He only calls his party﴾; that is, those whom he whispers to, so he exposes them to following him and turning away from Allah; ﴿that they may be﴾; by following him, firmly established; ﴿among the companions of the Blaze.﴾ This is his aim; he has no aim other than this. Yet he strives to conceal this from them, by making the aspect of hope prevail in their souls, causing them to forget the aspect of fear, showing them that repentance is in their hands, and postponing it for them by granting them room in hope and distance in the term, so as to corrupt their deeds. The Most Merciful, glorified is He, only calls His servants so that they may be among the people of bliss: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace﴾ [Yunus: 25].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 7:

When he had brought the exposition of the purpose of Satan to its conclusion, he drew attention to what He Himself, glorified is He, had decreed concerning his followers, by His saying, beginning a new statement: ﴿Those who disbelieve﴾; that is, they covered up (p-13) by following him in their desires what their intellects had pointed them to, and this clear exposition had uncovered for them to the utmost degree. ﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾; that is, in this world, through the loss of most of what they hope for, along with the scattering of their hearts, the blocking of their insight, the baseness of their aspirations, to the extent that they were content for their god to be a stone, and the veiling from them of the true knowledge, in which there is no real delight apart from it; and in the Hereafter, through the Blaze to which he invited them to keep company.

When He mentioned the recompense of His party, He followed it with the party of God, those who opposed their enemy, and said: ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾; that is, in confirmation of their faith, ﴿righteous deeds﴾. Since among the greatest snares of Satan is what befalls a person, through error and ignorance, of disobedience, because of the deficiency in him, so that he may drag him by that into deliberate transgression and aggression, He (exalted is He) said, calling him to His obedience and removing his shame: ﴿For them is forgiveness﴾; that is, a covering over of their sins, such that there is no punishment and no rebuke. This happens immediately in this abode; were it not for it, they would have been exposed, and tomorrow, were it not for it, they would have perished. And when He erased it in essence and trace, He affirmed the bounty, saying: ﴿And a great reward﴾; that is, one that is too immense to be described, beyond this general statement. Thus, part of it is immediate, through the ease of worship, the enduring of knowledge, and what they see in their hearts from beyond certainty; and part of it is deferred, through the realization of what is asked, from the great favour, and the attainment of what exceeds what is hoped for in Paradise.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 8:

(p-14) When this discourse made clear the disparity between the two parties in their final outcome, namely destruction and success, and no one with any sense would rush into destruction, and the unbelievers would claim that they are the successful ones, being satisfied with looking at their own state, and would claim that they are the most perceptive of people and the best in their deeds, and likewise every sinner and innovator, this was a cause for denying their equality. So He denied it, explaining the cause of their misguidance, in a way that provides consolation to the good-doers, an exhortation to thankfulness, and an urging to persist in need (of Allah) and humility, and in asking for well-being from slipping and deviation. So He said: ﴿Is then he﴾. And since the one who causes harm is the one who adorns (the evil), without regard to a specific agent, He framed His statement in the passive: ﴿to whom the evil of his deed is made attractive﴾, meaning its ugliness, which by its nature harms its doer, either immediately or in the end, through gathering perishable wealth, or wealth that will be left behind, without need; and through selling the comfort of everlasting Paradise for pursuit of a fleeting desire, and preferring a perishing created thing over his Lord, the Self-Sufficient, the Everlasting. Then He traced to it the ultimate end He had mentioned, saying: ﴿and he sees it﴾, i.e., the evil, because of the adornment, ﴿as good﴾, i.e., so he embraces it, by what the attaching of the deed to him indicates, and He omitted the comparison term; and it is like one who sees matters as they truly are, so he follows the good and avoids the evil, since the context points to this. And to hasten the removal of what was unclear to the hearer regarding the cause that leads one to see the ugly as beautiful, He said, emphasizing, refuting those who attribute any action, good or evil, to other than Allah: (p-15) ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, i.e., the cause of seeing things other than as they are is that ﴿Allah﴾, i.e., He to whom all command belongs, ﴿leads astray whom He wills﴾, so he sees nothing as it truly is, and so he rushes into clear destruction while seeing it as the very essence of salvation; ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾, so no matter is unclear to him, and He does nothing but good.

Since the lover is one who is pleased with the act of his beloved, He traced to this the prohibition addressed to the most perfect of His creation against grief because of their misguidance, in His saying: ﴿So let not﴾. The better view is to supply the comparison term here, so that the meaning becomes: "Is then one who has been deceived, who did evil and believed it good, because Allah has led him astray, by the cause that Allah is the one who turns hearts about, equal to one whom Allah has made to see the realities?" And since the answer is "No, they are not equal," He traced to it His saying: So let not ﴿your soul expire﴾, i.e., in death or what approaches it, ﴿in grief over them﴾, i.e., because of what they are in of blindness to clear matters, ﴿in sorrows﴾, i.e., for the sake of your successive regrets over their turning away; the plural of "ḥasrah," which is intense sorrow over what has passed of the matter.

Since it was as if it were said: "They harm Your friends, so their harm intensifies," and since the knowledge of the Powerful Friend of what His enemy does is sufficient for victory, He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, i.e., the One encompassing all attributes of perfection, ﴿is Knowing﴾, i.e., of perfect knowledge; and He emphasized it, alerting that the station is difficult, and whoever does not steady himself with the utmost of his effort slips, because of His (exalted be He) long respite for them and His forbearance toward them, ﴿of what they do﴾, i.e., of what they have been trained in and impressed upon, until it has become a disposition for them, from which their separation is extremely far.

[p. 16] When He (exalted is He) informed that the fulfilment of what He had promised must occur, namely the Resurrection and other things, and gave the strongest warning against being careless about His command, and denied the equating of the one who affirms it with the one who denies it, and when the cause of the misguidance that causes the hearts to die was desire (hawa), which covers the sky of the intellect and rises over it with its dark clouds, so that it prevents the intellect from penetrating, and when the cause of the clouds covering the sky of the earth, giving life to dead grains, was also desire, and when bringing it at one time rather than another indicated power exercised by choice, He said, linking (ʿatfan) to the clause "Indeed the promise of God is true," which is founded upon reflection, namely bringing into existence from non-existence, and clarifying His power over what He had promised, [He said]: ﴿And God﴾, that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, with no thing besides Him, neither nature nor anything else, ﴿is He who﴾. Since the intended meaning is bringing into existence from non-existence, He expressed it in the past tense, attributing it to Himself, because He is the true Agent. So He said: ﴿sends the winds﴾, that is, He brought them into existence from non-existence, agitated, having in them the capacity for agitation and motion, so that He may direct them however He wills, not fixed like the earth, and He placed them between the two horizons, for the good of the place of the earth.

Since their stirring is renewed whenever He wills to water a land, He said, attributing it to the winds because they are the cause, and expressing it in the present tense as a narration of the present state, so that that wondrous scene, which indicates the completeness of power, may be brought to mind, and thus the Arabs do with what is strange, to alert the listener to it and to urge him to contemplate and visualize it: ﴿so that they stir up﴾, that is, by His moving them when He wills; ﴿a cloud﴾, that is, He, glory be to Him, has established His practice that His wisdom should appear gradually.

Since the intended purpose is to infer the power to resurrect, and since the expression in the present tense repels obstinacy, He expressed it in the present tense. And since driving the cloud to one land rather than another, and watering one place rather than another, is of great majesty, He shifted (iltifat) from the third person (ghayba) and placed it in the mode of majesty, so He said: ﴿then We drive it﴾, that is, the cloud, expressing it in the past tense, to alert that every driving, whether in the past or the future, comes from Him alone, or through those whom He has appointed for that from His hosts, the angels or others, and not from other than Him. And He indicated that He distinguishes between distance and nearness by the particle of limit, so He said: ﴿to a dead land﴾.

Since the cause of life is the cloud, by what arises from it of water, He said: ﴿then We revive therewith the earth﴾. And since the intended purpose is to guide them to the power to resurrect, which they deny, He said, removing metaphor in every respect and clarifying the depiction in full: ﴿after its death﴾. When he had brought the matter to its conclusion, he increased the alerting to the blessing of the second bringing into existence by His saying: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like the reviving of the dead vegetation, ﴿is the resurrection﴾, sensibly for the dead and figuratively for the hearts and plants.

Al-Qushayri said: When He wishes to revive a heart, He first sends the winds of hope, and stirs up by them the hidden longings; then He produces in it a cloud of agitation and the anguish of restlessness; then the rain of truth comes, and it causes to grow in the heart the flowers of expansion and the lights of the spirit, and life becomes pleasant for its owner, until the subtleties of intimacy are completed.

When he had established all of this, what he had previously affirmed of His might and wisdom, and it was confirmed that He is able to resurrect, it followed that He has might in the Hereafter, as that was witnessed in this world. People compete for might, especially the disbelievers, more than they compete for wisdom. Whoever competes for wisdom is, in fact, competing for the sake of gaining might. The disbelievers only worshipped idols so that they might gain might through them, as He said: ﴿And they took besides Allah gods, that they might be for them a source of might﴾ [Maryam: 81]. He concluded from this, saying: ﴿Whoever﴾, i.e., at any time, ﴿desires might﴾, i.e., that he be needed by others while he is self-sufficient without them, mostly, and not overpowered. ﴿Then to Allah﴾, i.e., to Him alone, ﴿belongs all might﴾, i.e., let him seek it from Him, and not seek it from anyone else, for nothing else has any share in it. Whoever seeks something from other than its owner will be disappointed. Ibn al-Jawzi said: It has been narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed your Lord says every day: 'I am the Mighty; so whoever desires the might of both abodes, let him obey the Mighty.'"

(p-19) When he encouraged the pursuit of might, after informing that there is no share of it for anyone else, he indicated its exclusivity to Him through the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and power, and he explained that it is only attained through wisdom. So he said: ﴿To Him﴾, i.e., not to anyone else, ﴿ascends the good word﴾, i.e., that which proceeds according to the laws of the Sharia, with a good intention and sound belief, whether it is secret or public, because it is the very essence of wisdom, so it grants might to its speaker and rewards him.

When he raised the rank of the wise word, he explained that the deed is higher than it, because it is the intended goal in itself, and speech is a means to it. So he said, indicating its elevation by changing the style: ﴿And the righteous deed raises it﴾. He, glorified is He, Himself takes charge of raising it, and for its doer with Him is a firm might and an enduring bliss, and his deed succeeds. Al-Razi said, in al-Lawami': Knowledge is only completed through action, as it has been said: "Knowledge calls out to action; if it responds, well; otherwise it departs." End quote. And it has been said:

Do not be pleased with a man's sweet speech
until his conduct confirms what he says.

So when you weigh his speech against his conduct,
and they balance, then his friendship is beautiful.

When he explained what achieves might from wisdom, he explained what produces humiliation and brings about vengeance, from base aspiration. So he said: ﴿And those who plot﴾, i.e., who work in concealment (p-20) the evil schemes ﴿evil﴾, i.e., they conceal their intentions in them in order to carry them out suddenly. ﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾, just as they intended that for others. Their scheming does not rise to Him by itself, nor does He raise it, because it has no capacity for that, since it contradicts wisdom. Since what he mentioned of their scheming necessitates knowing its condition, whether it benefited them anything, He informed that He destroyed it by His might and annihilated it by His wisdom. So he said: ﴿And the scheming of those﴾, i.e., those far from success, ﴿it is﴾, i.e., He alone, not the scheming of one who intends good by his scheme, for Allah carries it out, exalts his affair, and grants him the final outcome, in fulfilment of His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And they scheme, and Allah schemes, and Allah is the best of schemers﴾ [al-Anfal: 30]. Just as He brought you out, O believers, from your homes for the sake of the caravan, so He brought the enemies out from their homes and placed them in the well of Badr. ﴿Will perish﴾, i.e., will be made worthless, will be corrupted, and will be destroyed. This indicates the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of good and evil, of speech and action, hidden and manifest, and the completeness of His power, and that is the meaning of "might." The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a device in which two opposites are mentioned and each is left implicit where the other is stated): it omitted what belongs to the doer of righteous deed and indicated it by mentioning what belongs to the doer of evil, and it omitted the raising of the evil scheme and indicated it by His raising of the righteous deed.

[p. 21] When He, glorified is He, mentioned what He had made them into, of divergence in character, He followed it with what they had been upon, of unity in the kind of origin. Their origin is dust, from which water is extracted after it has been mixed into the dust, even though its varieties differ. So He said, explaining some of the signs of the self (*ayat al-anfus*) and conjoining it to what He had conjoined it to, ﴿And it is Allah who sends the winds﴾ [Fatir: 9], which is among the signs of the horizons, alerting that He is able to distinguish after intense mixing, and that He has decreed everything: the provisions, the terms of life, the calamities, and the joys. So there is no fruit of scheming except what reaches the schemer of distress, punishment from Allah, and harm.

﴿And Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection. Since He left no need for restriction, He said: ﴿He created you from dust﴾, that is, a dust of the same kind, even though its varieties differ, through the creation of your father from it. He mixed it in a way that no one else could separate out. Then He transferred him from that substance as a fundamental origin and foundation. To this refers His saying ﴿then﴾, that is, after that in time and rank, ﴿He created you from a drop﴾ (*nutfah*), that is, He made it a second origin, of the same kind as that earthly origin, but more intimately mixed with it. Then, after completing the arrangement over a period of time and through stages, He brought you to the drop, which has no resemblance to dust, as proof of complete power and of acting by choice. ﴿Then He made you pairs﴾, between males and females, a sign more evident than what preceded it of choice, of the falsehood of the naturalists (*ahl al-tabā'i'*), and of resurrection, through distinguishing what from the dust is suited to maleness and femaleness.

Since pregnancy likewise refutes the naturalists, in that it does not occur from every intercourse, He pointed to it with His saying, emphasizing it as a refutation of them and as an announcement that this is only by His power: ﴿And no female bears﴾, that is, within the womb, through pregnancy, ﴿or gives birth﴾. The preposition (*min*) here indicates complete comprehensiveness. Since delivery is likewise such that it is not completed every time something is carried, He said ﴿except﴾ accompanied ﴿by His knowledge﴾ as to its time, its kind, its form, and other matters pertaining to it, exclusively concerning all of that, even from its mother, who is closest to it. So it does not occur except by His power. Whatever He wills, He completes, and whatever He wills, He brings forth.

Since what follows birth also indicates choice, through the differences among them in their life spans, while they are equal in reality, He indicated it with His saying, using the passive voice to show how easy the matter is for Him, glorified is He, and that the lengthening and shortening are the intended object of the attribution: ﴿And none is granted a lengthened life﴾, that is, has his life increased, meaning one whose life is long reaches longevity in actuality, perceptibly. Qatada said: "sixty years." Or it means, in meaning, by an increase by the choosing Agent, an increase which, were it not for it, his life would have been shorter than what he reached. ﴿Nor is any of his life shortened﴾, that is, of the one granted a lengthened life, in potentiality. This is the one who would ordinarily have been apt for a long life, but was not granted it through the diminishing by the choosing Agent, a diminishing which, were it not for it, his life would have been long. Thus the "one granted a lengthened life" mentioned here refers to the act, while the pronoun that returns to him refers to the one granted a lengthened life in potentiality. This is from the finest of the figure *badī' al-istikhdām* (the figure in which one term carries two referents). Had the expression been "one" (*aḥad*), this meaning would not be valid. The reading of Ya'qub, according to one of the transmissions from Ruways, with the *ya'* opened and the *qaf* vowelled with a *ḍamma*, in the active voice, shows that shortness of life is more frequent: ﴿وَلا يَنْقُصُ﴾.

Since this is in the context of knowledge, and the most precise means in our customary practices is writing, He said: ﴿except in a Book﴾, written in it: "The life of so-and-so is such-and-such; the life of so-and-so is such-and-such; and such-and-such is the life of so-and-so if he does such-and-such; and his life is such-and-such, more or less, if he does not do it."

Since that is a matter which counting cannot encompass and limits cannot confine, and so it is among what the ignorant deny, He said, emphasizing its ease: ﴿Indeed, that﴾, that is, this great matter of recording all the terms, decreeing them, and comprehending them in detail, ﴿for Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all might, so He overcomes everything He wills, exclusively, ﴿is easy﴾.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 12:

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned one of their two origins, the earth of varied kinds, He mentioned the other origin, water, which is more intermingled than earth. He noted the difference between its two kinds, which branch out into many varieties, drawing attention to His act by choice, and rebuking those who equate Him, glory be to Him, with anything so as to associate that thing with Him, despite the vast distance (p-24) beyond which there is no further distance, and despite the fact that these sensible things are distinguished from one another by some distance. So He said: ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾. Since the definite article (al-alif wa al-lam) is used for a known reference, He explained it by saying, pointing to the sweet one: ﴿This one is sweet﴾, that is, pleasant, sweet, delicious, agreeable to the nature; ﴿fresh﴾, that is, of extreme sweetness; ﴿palatable in its drinking﴾, that is, wholesome and easy to swallow, so that when it is drunk it passes down the throat without hindrance, and its swallowing is easy, because of the pleasure and agreeableness to the nature that it has. ﴿And this one is salty and bitter﴾, that is, it combines saltiness with bitterness, so its drink is not palatable; rather, if it were drunk, it would hurt the throat and kindle in the stomach what is like fire. The meaning is that He, glory be to Him, distinguished the two after bringing them together on the surface and in the depths of the earth, and did not let either of them transgress against the other. Rather, when a well is dug beside the salt sea, fresh and sweet water appears, in proportion to the soundness or corruption of the land.

Since salt water is impossible for a human being to drink, He mentioned that He created in it that by which life is sustained, equal in this to the sweet water. So He said: ﴿And from each you eat﴾, that is, from the salt and the sweet, ﴿fresh flesh﴾, that is, fish of various kinds, diversified into types beyond counting, and other than fish, ﴿fresh flesh﴾, that is, delightful to the palate. The saltiness did not harm what comes from the salt water with respect to its origin that you know, nor did the sweetness add to the pleasure of what comes from the sweet water, given its agreeableness to you. Since He mentioned among His bounties what is extremely soft, He followed it with what is extremely hard. So He said: ﴿And you extract﴾, that is, you seek to bring out from the salt water, but not from the sweet, and you find that for extraction. Al-Baghawi said: It has been said that pearls are attributed to both because there may be sweet springs within the salt sea that mix with it, so the pearl comes from that. ﴿Ornaments which you wear﴾, that is, your women wear them, from jewels, pearls, coral, and other things. Therefore, the softness of the one and the hardness of the other, together with the fact that both are generated from the same source, is decreed by none but the Doer who chooses.

Since eating and extraction are general benefits, He addressed them in general terms. But since the stability of something on the sea without sinking is a strange matter, which through its great familiarity is not perceived by anyone, except the people of insight, as one of the greatest signs pointing to the Capable, the Chooser, He addressed them specifically. So He said: ﴿And you see the ships﴾, that is, the boats. They are called "fulk" because of their circling, and "safinah" because of their cutting through the water. He placed the adverbial phrase first because it is more indicative of this, so He said: ﴿in it﴾, that is, in each of the two seas, ﴿plowing﴾, sinking into it, except a little of them. When the statement was complete, He mentioned their condition, which is explained by seeking, so He said: ﴿gliding﴾ (p-26), that is, running, turning away from the wind, cutting the water, piercing the air with their prows. This one comes forward and that one goes backward, its face toward the back of the other, by one and the same wind. Al-Bukhari, in the chapter on trade by sea, said: Mujahid said: The ships cut through the wind, and the wind does not cut through the ships except the great ships. The author of al-Qamus said: "Makharat al-safinatu (like mana'a) makhran wa mukhuran": it ran; or it faced the wind in its course; and "al-fulk al-mawakhir" are those whose sound of running is heard, or which cut the water with their prows, or which go forward and backward with one and the same wind. In a hadith: "When one of you wants to urinate, let him face the wind (fal-yatamakhkhar al-rih)." In another wording: "Istamkhiru al-rih," that is, make your backs toward the wind, for when one turns his back to it, it cuts through him with his back, and it takes from his right and left. It may also be that facing it is "tamakhkhur," but in the hadith it is turning the back. End of al-Qamus. Then he connected the "makhr" with a reason, saying: ﴿that you may seek﴾, that is, seek earnestly. Since the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam) was mentioned in the verse before it, He returned the pronoun to it, so that the strength of the connection between this verse and the one before it may be known. So He said: ﴿of His bounty﴾, that is, of Allah, by reaching through this distant lands for trade and other purposes. Had He made them still, this would not have followed from them. In Surat al-Jathiyah there is something useful here. ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾, that is, so that your state with these blessings, which point to the great power and kindness of Allah, may be the state of one from whom gratitude is hoped (p-27).

When He (glory be to Him) mentioned the difference in the essences, which points to the wondrous artistry of His creation, He followed it with the alternation of the two states, as a sign of His perfect power. He said, in a position of circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "He created you," indicating that God (exalted is He) fashioned Adam when He created the earth, before there was night or day. Then He breathed the spirit into him on the last day of Friday, after He had created light on Wednesday. So no period of time came upon man, which is the measure of the movement of the celestial sphere, except that he was "a thing not worth mentioning."

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day﴾: that is, He makes it enter, by way of circulation, so the darkness becomes light.

Since this act is most astonishing, and because it has become familiar through its frequent repetition, so that people have become heedless of what it shows of complete power, He drew attention to it by repeating the verb, saying: ﴿and He causes the day to enter into the night﴾, so that what was light becomes darkness. Sometimes the alternation is by the shortening of this and the lengthening of that. All of this shows that He (exalted is He) acts by choice.

When He mentioned the two alternating phases, He mentioned what arises from them, saying: ﴿And He has subjected the sun and the moon﴾. Then He resumed His speech: ﴿each﴾, that is, of them, ﴿runs﴾. Since the aim of the surah is the completeness of power, and the context here is about compelling disparate things to what He wills, and since He ended the verse with the word "dominion" (al-mulk), which looks to compulsion and subjugation, the particle of ending (harf al-ghayah) was not suitable for this place. So He said: ﴿for a term﴾, that is, for a term ﴿specified﴾, appointed for it, which it cannot exceed. When that term comes, it sets; so every day, until the greatest term comes, and then this whole order is disrupted, by the command of the King, the All-Knowing, and He raises people for the Day of Crowding, and the great matters will occur.

When He (glory be to Him) had shown, by what every person witnesses in himself and in others, that He is the Doer who chooses, able to do whatever He wills, and concluded with what is repeatedly witnessed twice every day, this produced, as a certainty, His saying, magnifying Himself with the particle of distance and the plural mim: ﴿That is﴾, that is, the One of exalted rank, who did all these acts; ﴿God﴾, that is, the One who possesses every attribute of perfection. Then He alerted them that there is no governor for them besides Him, by another predicate, saying: ﴿your Lord﴾, that is, the One who brought you into existence from non-existence, who nurtures you with all blessings; there is no lord for you besides Him. Then He resumed His speech: ﴿His is the dominion﴾, that is, He alone; ﴿the dominion﴾, that is, all of it; He is the owner of everything. ﴿And those you call upon﴾, that is, with the call of worship; then He clarified their station by His saying: ﴿besides Him﴾, that is, the idols and others, and everything else, which is beneath Him (glory be to Him); ﴿they do not own﴾, that is, in this state in which you call upon them, and in every state in which this speech can be addressed to you. He went to the extreme in negation, and said: ﴿not even a qitmir﴾. It is, as related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both), (p-٢٩) the thin membrane around the date-stone, the delicate skin wrapped around it, as a metaphor for the smallest of things; so how much more for what is above it? They have no share of dominion at all. So the verse is an instance of al-ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which something is mentioned in one part and omitted in its counterpart): it mentioned "dominion" first, as evidence of its omission second; and the absence of dominion second, as evidence of its omission first.

Then He explained this by His saying: ﴿If you call upon them﴾; that is, the objects of worship other than Him, [calling upon them] in worship or in seeking aid; ﴿they do not hear﴾; that is, with the sense of hearing; at any time; ﴿your call﴾; because they are inanimate; ﴿and even if they heard﴾; in the future; ﴿they would not respond to you﴾; because at that time they would know that your response would not please God; and they are among those who refused to bear the trust and betray it by acting in a way that does not please God, the Exalted; or the meaning is: even if it were supposed that they have hearing, or even if they were hearing, so as to include those among the living who are worshipped, hearing would not necessarily entail response, because there is no necessary connection between hearing and speech, together with the ability to do what is demanded of the hearer; for beasts hear and respond, and those who respond other than Him respond without having the ability to do most of what is asked of them.

When He mentioned what is by way of supposition, He mentioned what their affair will come to between them and Him, saying: ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾; that is, when God makes them speak (p-30) ﴿they will disavow your partnership﴾; that is, they will deny it and disown it. Since the implicit sense was: "The One Who is Aware has informed you of this," and they did not acknowledge this, nor understand it as it should be understood, nor act upon it, He turned the address away from them to the One who has complete understanding and perfect obedience, and said, linking to what the context guided us to supply: ﴿And none can inform you like the One who is Aware﴾; that is, with an eloquent and great informing in this manner, concerning anything at all; ﴿like the One who is Aware﴾; that is, one who has far-reaching knowledge of news; so it is impossible to find fault with anything He has informed of; whereas others, when they report any news, are open to a defect being attributed to them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 15:

When He (glory be to Him) was singled out for dominion, and denied that their partners had any benefit, this produced His saying: ﴿O mankind, you are the poor﴾; that is, all of you; ﴿you﴾; that is, specifically; ﴿the poor﴾; that is, because of the breadth of your knowledge, the spread of your thoughts and the dispersal of your minds, your impulses multiply and your motives scatter, so your need grows greatly, due to the intensity of your weakness and incapacity, to a degree that the need of others is counted as nonexistent alongside it. Had the predicate been indefinite, this meaning would not have been conveyed. ﴿To Allah﴾; that is, the One to whom belongs all dominion. Al-Qushayri said: Poverty is of two kinds: poverty of creation (faqr khilqah) and poverty of attribute (faqr sifah). The first is general: every created thing is in need of its Creator at the first moment of its existence, so that He may bring it into being and make it grow, and at its subsequent moments, so that He may sustain it and keep it in existence. As for poverty of attribute, it is detachment. The poverty of the common people is detachment from wealth, and the poverty of the elite is detachment from [seeking] causes. Thus the true praiseworthy poverty is the detachment of the innermost heart from dependent things.

When He reminded the servant of his true attribute, He followed it with mention of the Creator by His greatest name, closely after mentioning the aspect by which he was described with what was mentioned, which is comprehensiveness of the attributes of perfection. So He said: ﴿And Allah is the One﴾; that is, alone; ﴿the Self-Sufficient﴾; that is, the One who cannot be conceived as needing anything: not you, nor your worship, nor anything at all. Since a self-sufficient creature's sufficiency does not embrace whoever seeks it, and if it embraces them, its giving does not embrace them, out of fear of poverty or other accidents, and the generality of its blessing cannot be realized in any particular thing, its self-sufficiency is never free of some kind of blame. Praise, as al-Harrali said in his explanation of the Names, is the goodness of totality through the completion of every matter, part and portion of it to the end of its perfection. Whenever a part of a whole falls short of its perfect end, that whole is not praiseworthy, and its sustainer is not praiseworthy. Allah created every thing as it should be and did not hasten anything before its proper time and measure. Blame is a deficiency that attaches to some parts for one who has not seen them in their entirety nor seen all of them; so blame occurs only in a restricted sense, when taken as a fragment of a whole, while praise occurs only in a whole from which nothing has departed. There is no praise in a part, nor blame in a whole, and there is no praise except in a whole. For this reason al-Ghazali said: The praiseworthy among servants is the one whose habits, character and actions are all praised, without any reservation.

Since He (glory be to Him) had bestowed His blessings upon His creation, and made them abundant, both apparent and hidden, and had given them the capacity to receive them, which nothing prevents except His own power: ﴿And the giving of your Lord is never restricted﴾ [al-Isra: 20]; and since what He possesses is never diminished, His giving is praise and His withholding is praise, for He does not withhold for a purpose, but for a wisdom too subtle for thoughts. So He said: ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾; that is, everything is in His favor by His blessing, and He is deserving of praise in Himself. From this there follows, decisively, a threat to whoever disobeys Him and a severe warning:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 16:

﴿If He wills, He can remove you all﴾; i.e., all of you; ﴿and bring a new creation﴾; i.e., other than you; for ﴿He is over all things competent﴾;

"And that" — that is, the great matter — of removing and bringing (in its place) — "is not difficult for Allah" — the One encompassing all attributes of perfection in particular — "[anything] unattainable" — that is, [nothing] impossible or burdensome. And it is praiseworthy in the case of annihilation just as it is praiseworthy in the case of creation.

﴿Wa-la﴾; that is, [Allah] will not remove you as a punishment for your sins and as a sign of power over you, while the state is that no bearer of burdens ﴿taziru﴾, that is, bears [a burden] on the Day of Resurrection, or at the time of removal. Since no soul fit to bear a burden is free of some burden it carries, and "the protected" (al-ma'sum) is one whom Allah protects, He said: ﴿wazira﴾, rather than "nafs" (soul), meaning no bearer bears, from the aspect of sin, ﴿wizra﴾, that is, a load and weight, ﴿ukhra﴾, so that it may be punished for it. Rather, each one of you has, from what his hands have earned, whatever the proof is established against him for the punishment, whether directly or by causation, despite your differing in burden. No one bears anything except what he himself has committed. No soul is seized for another's sin that belongs to that other soul, as the tyrants of this world do.

Since He had established that no one is seized except for a burden, and had negated that anyone bears the burden of another, and since this might be taken to apply only to certain states or certain persons, and since the greatness of a burden requires the greatness of the punishment, He removed that misunderstanding. He indicated the ability to make them differ in reward, even if their seizing occurs at one moment, by His saying: ﴿wa-in tad'u﴾, that is, a soul; ﴿muthqalah﴾, that is, weighed down with sins, whether they are disbelief or otherwise; calling anyone ﴿ila himliha﴾, that is, to its own specific load of sins, which are not borne by another through direct action or causation, so that it might lighten [the load] for it, and thus the punishment is lightened in accordance with its lightness; ﴿la yuhmal﴾, that is, not carried by any carrier at all; ﴿minhu shay'un﴾, that is, not willingly nor unwillingly. Rather, each person has a matter that occupies him, essentially and causally. ﴿Wa-law kana﴾, that is, that caller or the one called to bear [the load], ﴿dha qurba﴾, to the one who called him. The essence of the first [clause] is that no one perishes for another's sin, but for his own sin; and the essence of the second is that no one's sin is lifted from him so that he may be saved.

Since this matter, despite being clear, strips hearts [of their composure], so that the listener's astonishment at one who hears it and yet does not fear becomes intense, He said, removing this wonder by way of the conclusion (natijah): ﴿Innama tundhiru﴾, that is, a warning that results in turning back from error. Because they alone benefit from it, they are as if they were exclusively the ones warned. It is, as al-Qushayri said, "the informing of the place of fear." ﴿Alladhina yakhshawna﴾, that is, those who actually perform this act in the present, and persist in it for the future. Since the most intelligent of people is one who fears the Benefactor, because the least of His punishment is the cutting off of His favour, He said: ﴿rabbahum﴾.

Since the most perfect of people in intellect, the highest in resolve, and the most noble in origin is one whose absence is like his presence, and who, with the caller's words, what appears to him of his bearing, and the beauty of his speech and action, does not need a sign to display or an extraordinary event to bring forth, but whose faith is confirmation of the caller's report of the unseen matter, without any uncovering of a veil, He said: ﴿bil-ghayb﴾, that is, while they are absent from what they were called to and warned about; or while He is absent from them; or while they are absent from one whose display [of piety] might be feigned. Thus they are equally sincere in their fear, such that none beholds them except Allah. We know of no one who equalled Khadijah and al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with both of them, in this.

Since prayer comprises the submission of both the outward and the inward, and so it is the noblest of acts of worship, and since establishing it in the sense of observing all its limits in every state is the strongest proof of sincerity, He said, using the past tense because the times of prayer are fixed: ﴿wa-aqamu al-salah﴾, that is, as evidence of their fear; ﴿al-salah﴾ at its five appointed times, along with what follows of its recommended practices (sunan).

Since the implied sense is: whoever is not of this state has been corrupted (tadassa), and whoever is of this state has purified himself (tazakka), and whoever is corrupted is only corrupting himself, He followed this with His saying, indicating by the form of the verb with the reflexive prefix (tafa''ul, i.e. the tafa''ala verb form) that the soul is most inclined to filth, and so it does not submit to the best correction except through great striving: ﴿wa-man tazakka﴾, that is, purifies himself and increases through these good qualities. Since a person, because of the proximate causes, may overlook that this is a benefit to him and specific to him, He emphasized it, saying: ﴿fa-innama yatazakka li-nafsihi﴾, for it neither harms nor benefits, in reality, anything other than itself. ﴿Wa-ila Allah﴾, who reveals all His attributes with the fullest disclosure the intellects can bear on the Day of Resurrection, not to anyone else, ﴿al-masir﴾, just as the origin was from Him. So He will recompense each person for his deed, and will judge justly between you and the one who feared his Lord through your warning, and the one who turned away from that.

(p-36) When the intended sense was: "So neither is equal in nature and intellect, the one who has corrupted himself (al-mudassi), who is blind through his disobedience in the darknesses, nor the one who has purified himself (al-mutazakki), who through his acts of obedience is seeing in the light, even though the two are equal in humanity," he followed this with what is suitable as examples of the one who corrupts and the one who purifies, and of what brings about corruption and purification. This shows the completeness of His power, to which the context has pointed since the beginning of the surah, and it affirms that fear and hardness are in His hand, refuting the view of those who attribute affairs to natures. This is his saying: ﴿And not equal﴾, that is, in any state whatsoever. Since the purpose was to admonish the polytheists, and the one who corrupts (al-mudassi) comes before the one who purifies (al-mutazakki), as he had established earlier, it was fitting to arrange his saying in this order, as examples of the disbeliever and the believer, the ignorant and the knowing. He mentioned the example of the ignorant first, because the origin of sending messengers is ignorance: ﴿the blind and the seeing﴾, that is, neither the two categories, nor their individuals, nor the individuals of one category of them. The clear variation among the individuals of each of the two categories made it unnecessary to repeat the negation. So the meaning is that people are not equal in blindness and sight; rather, some are blind and some are seeing. The verb "iftaʿala" (افتعل) here carries the sense of "tafaʿala" (تفاعل). Perhaps he used it to indicate negation, though an effort was made to avoid it, or to indicate that what is negated is equality in every respect, not in the basic meaning. Had this been based on nature, they would have been on a single path. Rather, the individuals within each category vary: you find some of the blind walking without a guide through confusing alleys, another unable to walk in his own house except with a guide, and another who, when he touches a book, perceives how many lines his ruler covers from a line and whether its handwriting is good or not. (p-37) Another recognizes a counterfeit dirham from a genuine one and distinguishes the minting of each land from others, and perhaps someone disputes with him by sophistry, yet he does not accept the doubt; and another is at the furthest extreme from all of that. As for the seeing, the matter is evident in them, in the variation of their sight and their insight. All of this is clear evidence that the Agent is capable and choosing, adding to creation whatever He wills; otherwise the individuals would be equal and they would all be on a single path.

When this was among the most wondrous of matters, though people overlook it because of its familiarity, He drew attention to its wonder and to the greater manifestation of power in it, by repeating the negative particle with its counterparts. He also drew attention to the fact that sight penetrates only in darkness, as a reminder that sins darken the heart of the believer even when he is perceptive. He placed the darkness first because it more clearly shows the difference in sight, and this fits the context, as has been established. So He said, in coordinating pair with pair and single with single, comprehensively, as a reminder that the paths of misguidance cannot be counted: ﴿and not the darknesses﴾, which are an example of falsehoods. He emphasized it by repeating the negative particle, as with the previous one, because the difference between the individual kinds of darkness and the individual kinds of light is subtle. He said, drawing attention to the fact that the path to the truth is one, and refuting those of the zanadiqa (heretics) who said, "The paths to God are as numerous as the breaths of creatures": ﴿nor the light﴾, which is an example of the truth. So none but God (exalted is He), the Doer who chooses, could have originated these two opposites in this way. He made the individual kinds of light (p-38) and the individual kinds of darkness differ: the light of the sun does not resemble the light of the moon, and neither of them resembles the light of other stars, and none of these resembles the light of a lamp, and so on through the other kinds of light. If you consider the individual kinds of darkness, you will find them to be likewise, for darknesses are only shadows, and some shadows are denser than others.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 21:

Since darkness arises from shadows, and shadow is the cancellation of light, he (God) placed it first. So He said, putting forward the example of good, because mercy precedes wrath: ﴿Nor is the shade﴾; that is, with its coolness, which is the destination of the believer in the Hereafter; ﴿nor the scorching heat﴾; that is, with its blaze, which is the destination of the disbeliever. Al-Baghawi said: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: it is the hot wind at night. Likewise said the Qamus (al-Qamus al-Muhit by al-Fayruzabadi), and he added: it may also be during the day, the heat of the sun, the constant heat, and the fire. Thus the judgment of natures is definitively negated.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 22:**

Since life is what manifests all of that, he put it first and said, as another example for the believers. For this reason he repeated the verb. This example is above the example of the blind and the seeing, because the blind man shares the seeing man's perception in some respects. The believer and the disbeliever have two examples, so that the first (the example of the living and the dead) denies that the genus is equal to the genus while allowing judgment on individuals, and the second is the reverse: it denies equality among individuals while allowing it for the genus. ﴿And the living are not equal﴾: that is, because among them there is the one who speaks and the one who does not speak (the mute), the intelligent and the dull, the easy and the difficult, so that hardly any two living beings are alike in all qualities. ﴿Nor the dead﴾: that is, those who are the example of the disbelievers in the difficulty and ease of death, in decay, and in other things that are hidden and that the disbelievers do not acknowledge, in terms of wretchedness and felicity. (p-39)

Since what has been mentioned in this manner, with its clarity of indication that the act is by choice and that those who associate anything with Him are astray, because nothing resembles Him, is in a position with no obscurity, and with such firmness that no speech comes near it, the hearer is astonished at the one who refuses it. So He said, removing that astonishment and affirming that fear and hardness are only in His hand, and that warning is only for the one whom He has decreed to benefit, consoling His Prophet (ﷺ), emphasizing, and refuting whoever attributes to anyone other than Him, glorified is He, an act of good or evil: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾: that is, the One able to differentiate between these things, and over all things, with the comprehensiveness of the attributes of perfection that He has. He expressed it with the verb, to indicate the power to do that at every time He wills, glorified is He, so He said: ﴿He causes to hear whom He wills﴾: that is, guiding him, even if he did not ordinarily have the capacity, like inanimate objects; ﴿and you cannot cause to hear those who are in the graves﴾ no, wait, the text reads: and He makes deaf whom He wills, so He blinds him, overturns him, and destroys him, from the living of hearts and spirits and the dead of meanings and forms. The meaning is that if their hearing were based on natures they would be equal, either in responding or in turning away, because the attribution of the call and the manifestation of the miracle to them is on one equal footing. So the verse confirms the verse: ﴿You only warn those who fear their Lord unseen﴾ [Fatir: 18].

Since the one who turns away has equated himself with the dead in his state, which is not benefiting from what he sees and hears of extraordinary signs, and so he is as if he were dead, He said, expressing it in the nominal (ismiyyah) form, to alert to the non-affirmation of that for him (ﷺ): ﴿And you are not﴾: that is, by yourself, without Allah enabling you; and it is more emphatic in negation, so He said: ﴿one who causes to hear﴾: that is, in any way; ﴿those who are in the graves﴾: that is, the physical and the figurative dead; causing them to hear in a way that benefits them. Rather, Allah causes them to hear if He wills, so do not let your soul go in pursuit of them in regret. The verse is evidence for the Resurrection.

Since this is the prerogative of God, He indicated its negation for Him, limiting the description to warning, as an indication that most of creation have hearts that are dead. So He said, emphasizing the refutation of those who suppose that the warner is able to guide, or to other than that, except by His empowering him: ﴿Not﴾; that is, "not"; ﴿you are but a warner﴾; that is, you alert dead hearts with the striking blows of warning, and you are not a guardian who compels them to faith.

When he (ﷺ) was a Prophet of mercy, and restricting the description to this attribute might have given a wrong impression, he followed it, to make clear his greatness (ﷺ), with a shift (al-iltifat, a change of grammatical person) to the locus of greatness, because the greatness of the Messenger derives from the greatness of the One who sent him. Thus his warning is itself mercy. He says: ﴿Indeed We have sent you﴾, that is, with the greatness We possess; ﴿sent you﴾, that is, to this community; sent with ﴿the truth﴾, that is, with a matter perfect in its firmness, which reality corresponds to. For whoever considers the abundance of the proofs he was given will know that reality agrees with what he commands. Expressing it as a verbal noun (taqdir bil-masdar) conveys that the message is truth, and that both the Sender and the Messenger are in the right. ﴿A bringer of good tidings﴾, that is, to whoever obeys; ﴿and a warner﴾, that is, to whoever disobeys. The conjunction with waw indicates the nobility of each of the two attributes.

Since consolation (al-ta'si, consoling the Prophet) is among the things that ease leading and weaken resistance, He said, emphasizing it to repel the notion that sending to all nations is unlikely: ﴿And there is no nation﴾, that is, while the situation is that there is not, among the past nations, ﴿but a warner has passed among them﴾, whom We sent to them as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, either in person, or through what he left among their descendants of his laws, including his sayings, his deeds, and his traditions, together with the intellects they possess that testify to this. Warning implies good tidings, and He restricted the mention to it because it is by warning that consolation is achieved, given the hardship it entails. Also, among the earlier Prophets, peace be upon them, there was one whose mission was purely that of warning, because none benefited from his good tidings, since none of them followed him.

(p-42) Since he (ﷺ) was intensely grieved over their turning away, out of compassion for them and out of fear that this might be due to a shortcoming in his own conduct, and the implied sense was: "So if they believe you, it is their share in this world and the Hereafter," He (Exalted) followed it with, to console and comfort him, His words: ﴿And if they deny you, then [be consoled]﴾; that is, be consoled, for ﴿those before them denied﴾. Since those who denied were some of the people, it necessarily follows that they existed at some time, so He indicated this by the prepositional phrase and said: ﴿before them﴾; that is, what their messengers brought them from Allah.

Since the acceptance by the messengers of what came to them from Allah, and the negation of any shortcoming in their conveying of it, indicate the exaltedness of their station and the lowliness of the matter of the deniers among the nations, and all of this indicates the perfection of Allah's (Exalted) power in differentiating among creatures, He said, indicating both the matters of exaltedness and lowliness, as a new sentence answering one who might ask: "Was their denial out of obstinacy, or due to a deficiency in the clarity of the message?": ﴿Their messengers came to them with the clear proofs﴾; that is, the clear signs that are evident in indicating the truthfulness of the message. Since belief in the Book is binding on everyone whose command has reached him, and attributing denial to all the nations is a strange matter, the matter was worthy of emphasis, lest it be thought that they denied only because the Book was absent. So He emphasized it by repeating the preposition (p-43), and said: ﴿and with the scriptures﴾; that is, the written matters, from the pages and the like, and the ways and secrets; ﴿and with the Book﴾; that is, the genre of Book, such as the Torah and the Gospel; ﴿the illuminating﴾; that is, clear in itself, making clear the path of good and evil. Just as you came to your people with the like of that, even though your path is clearer and more manifest, and your Book is more luminous, more dazzling, more evident, and more widely known.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 35, verse 26:

When He had consoled him, He threatened those who opposed and disobeyed him, by what He did to those nations. So He said, turning the speech toward individuals to repel every confusion, and indicating with the particle of delay (thumma) that the length of respite should be a cause for turning back in repentance, not for being deceived by the assumption of neglect: ﴿Then I seized those who disbelieved﴾; that is, with various kinds of seizing; ﴿those who disbelieved﴾; that is, who concealed those clear signs, after the long patience of the messengers with them and their calling them (to faith).

Since the seizing of those whose stories were recounted among the Arabs was well known, and it took forms of punishment that were astonishing, He made the question a consequence of it, by His saying: ﴿So how was My rejection?﴾; that is, My rejecting them; meaning that it is a rejection whose manner must be asked about, because of its terror and its magnitude. As al-Qushayri said: "And if they persist in their way of error, you will not find any change in Our way regarding vengeance and disgrace."

[p. 44] Since it is among the most wondrous things that indicate the perfection of power, which in turn indicates the Oneness (*al-wahdaniyyah*, the oneness of God), that one single thing should be the cause of the happiness and guidance of one people, and of the wretchedness, misguidance and blindness of another, and since this is a subtle matter and a grave affair, which none grasps in its true understanding except the highest of creation, He, glory be to Him, reminded the addressee, by this mention, of what he witnesses of His signs. He said, in the form of a question (*al-istikhbar*, interrogative form), in order to bring the addressee to the rank of those endowed with understanding, with what He had introduced of that, glory be to Him, in the form of a statement, in His saying: ﴿And Allah is the One who sends the winds﴾ [Fatir: 9]. He turned the speech to the Greatest Name (*al-ism al-a'zam*, the Greatest Name of God), indicating the greatness of what is within its sphere: ﴿Do you not see that Allah﴾, that is, the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection; ﴿sends down from the sky﴾, that is, the sky to which water does not ascend, and which does not hold back from descending from it at times other than their appointed times, except by a overpowering power that nothing can frustrate; ﴿water﴾, that is, there is nothing resembling it in the sameness of some of it to others, so no one other than Him, glory be to Him, has the power to distinguish any part of it as suitable for one thing and not another.

Since this is a matter beyond the faculties of the intellects, He drew attention to it by the shift (*al-iltifat*, shift in grammatical person) to the locus of greatness, and said: ﴿then We bring forth﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness; ﴿thereby﴾, that is, by the water; ﴿from the earth﴾; ﴿fruits﴾, that is, of many kinds; ﴿of varying colours﴾, that is, the colours of their kinds, their categories, their forms and their natures.
